item.title: Keenan Allen formally charged with two misdemeanors from August arrest
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Colts wide receiver Keenan Allen has been formally charged with a pair of misdemeanors related to his August arrest on suspicion of driving under the influence.
item.content:encoded:
Colts wide receiver Keenan Allen has been formally charged with a pair of misdemeanors related to his August arrest on suspicion of driving under the influence.

According to multiple reports, Allen has been formally charged with with operating a vehicle with an alcohol concentration equivalent (ACE) of 0.15 or more and operating a vehicle while intoxicated. The former charge is a Class A misdemeanor which carries a possible jail sentence of up to one year and a fine of no more than $5000. The other charge can result in a jail term of no more than 60 days and a fine of no more than $500.

Colts General Manager Chris Ballard said that any team discipline would be handled internally. Allen also faces possible league discipline, which is typically a three-game suspension for alcohol-related offenses. Nathan Brown of the Indianapolis Star notes that the collective bargaining agreement allows for enhanced penalties given Allen's ACE level.

Allen played in last Sunday's loss to the Ravens and had six catches for 32 yards.

item.title: Could Carson Wentz play his way into the Vikings' QB1 job?
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Wentz performed well in Week 1. If it continues, the Vikings could stick with the hot hand.
item.content:encoded:
Most casual observers of the NFL were surprised to see quarterback Carson Wentz enter Sunday's game for the Vikings after Kyler Murray suffered a concussion on the third drive of the game. There's another potential surprise in the pipeline.

If Wentz keeps playing well and winning, he could end up hanging onto the job even after Murray is cleared to return.

Ian Rapoport of NFL Network floated that idea on Tuesday night. And it would be a stunner; Wentz was never in the competition to start, if the competition between Murray and J.J. McCarthy was even a real competition. (It likely wasn't.)

Last year, when Wentz was playing in place of McCarthy, who suffered an ankle sprain in Week 2, there was a sense that Wentz could keep the job even after McCarthy was ready to play. The key factor in that was simple — Wentz and receiver Justin Jefferson had a more effective in-game connection than McCarthy and Jefferson.

A season-ending injury to Wentz's left shoulder, through which he played for multiple weeks, ended that debate. This year, a fresh debate could emerge — if Murray can't return for Sunday's game against the Bears and if Wentz can engineer an upset at Soldier Field.

Rapoport calls the possibility an "excellent problem." Still, the best problem is no problem at all. It won't be easy to manage Murray if he believes he lost his job over a concussion suffered on the third drive of the opening game of the season.

In the end, however, it's all about winning games. If Wentz keeps winning, maybe he'll keep playing.

Either way, the Vikings have a pair of top-two draft picks who grew up rooting for the team. Murray, for now, isn't healthy enough to play. Wentz is. He'll get an opportunity to extend his run if he can continue to run the offense in a way that helps Minnesota score more points than the other team.

Which, in a numbers-driven league, continues to be the only statistic that matters.

item.title: Packers sign WR Bo Melton to active roster
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Wide receiver Bo Melton is back on the 53-man roster in Green Bay.
item.content:encoded:
Wide receiver Bo Melton is back on the 53-man roster in Green Bay.

Melton was released late last week and re-signed to the practice squad ahead of Sunday's loss to the Vikings. He was elevated to play in the game and saw action on both offense and special teams.

Melton caught one pass for 10 yards and returned four kickoffs over the course of the afternoon. That was his 39th appearance with the Packers since joining the team in December 2022.

The Packers also announced that they have released long snapper Scott Daly from the practice squad. Daly did not take part in Sunday's loss.

item.title: Marshall Faulk acknowledges the reality of early-season "crash-test dummy" games
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The new age of college football has made one of its time-honored traditions even more glaring — the early-season tuneup games.
item.content:encoded:
The new age of college football has made one of its time-honored traditions even more glaring — the early-season tuneup games.

First-year Southern coach Marshall Faulk witnessed it on Saturday, when No. 22-ranked Houston shredded his Jaguars, 77-6.

"That wasn't really a game, that was kind of a preseason crash-dummy test for Houston to work on all the good plays," Faulk told reporters, via Brad Crawford of CBS Sports.

Southern was paid $450,000 to serve as the cannon fodder for the Cougars.

For decades, high-level programs have scheduled lower-level schools in the early weeks of the season. What used to be games between Division I-A and Division I-AA have become FBS vs. FCS slaughterhouses.

"Let's just be real, OK?" Faulk said. "They're better than us. We're FCS, everybody knows what this is, let it be what it is."

The transfer portal has made matters worse, because the best young players at FCS schools typically end up getting big bucks with FBS programs.

"I was literally standing on the sideline thinking to myself, back when let's say Southern had juniors and seniors . . . this could be a competitive game playing a team like Houston," Faulk said. "In today's landscape, we don't have the budget to compete against them. We just don't."

Saturday's game included an eight-minute fourth quarter, after Houston built a 70-0 lead through the first 45 minutes.

"The reality is our kids were giving their best effort, but we're not good enough to beat a team that doesn't beat themselves," Faulk said. "There's not anything we could've done. I've been around a lot of football, man. We don't have the bodies, we don't have the funds, we don't have the equipment . . . all the stuff needed to compete with a team like that. . . . Guts and glory and want and will is not enough to compete with a team like that."

Again, it's been that way for a long time. Recent trends have made it worse. The question becomes whether the powers-that-be will change the rules to prevent games like this from happening.

The problem is that, even if the players have no business going against elite programs, their schools won't want to give up the revenue that comes from serving as a sacrificial lamb.

item.title: DeMeco Ryans on Texans defense: I don't believe in hype, this isn't 2025, we have to earn it
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: Leading up to the 2026 season, there was plenty of talk about how good the Texans defense could be — that the unit could help lead Houston to a deep postseason run.
item.content:encoded:
Leading up to the 2026 season, there was plenty of talk about how good the Texans defense could be — that the unit could help lead Houston to a deep postseason run.

But then Week 1 happened, with the Texans letting up 409 yards and 36 points in the loss to the Bills.

Buffalo does have one of the league’s best quarterbacks in Josh Allen and continuity on offense with former coordinator Joe Brady getting promoted to head coach. So the Bills have the potential to do that to many teams.

Still, it was a disappointing opening for a team that finished No. 1 in yards allowed and No. 2 in points allowed last year.

So did the Texans buy into the offseason hype too much? Did they consume the proverbial rat poison?

“I don't know,” head coach DeMeco Ryans said in his Monday press conference, via transcript from the team. “You have to ask those guys about the hype. I don't believe in hype. You've heard me stand here many times and talk about people talking about how great the defense was. Yeah, that was 2025. You don't just line up, and it's 2026, and just because you were good last year, you got to go out and make the plays. We made plays.

“The difference in this game on Sunday, versus the time we played the guys last year, we took the ball away three times. We go into this game, we don't take the ball away at all. We turn the ball over two times and we don't play smart defensively. We're not where we're supposed to be. We know the quarterback is going to scramble out to our left — if we don't stay out to our left and the quarterback runs for a touchdown, they're going to make plays.”

Ryans added that whatever Houston does this year, it’s not about how good the unit has been in the past.

“You have to put your stamp each and every year on who you're going to be,” Ryans said. “This is a new team. This isn't 2025. You have to go earn it. That's every year in the league, you have to go prove yourself. You can talk about it all you want to, how good you want to be, what are you going to do. You have to go out and make plays.

“That's always been my message. My message never changes. Talk never matters. When the ball is snapped, what are you doing?”

The Texans will be challenged defensively once again in Week 2, as the Bengals will be in town to face the club at 1 p.m. ET.

item.title: Bills and Texans each fumbled twice, Bills recovered all four on way to 36-31 win
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Bills coach Joe Brady cited the importance of O'Cyrus Torrence recovering James Cook's fumble on the game-winning drive.
item.content:encoded:
The Bills' 36-31 win over the Texans could have gone the other way if some fumbled footballs had bounced a little differently.

Both teams fumbled twice in the game, and the Bills recovered all four fumbles. In a one-possession game that was decided when the Bills recovered C.J. Stroud's second fumble with nine seconds left, any one of those fumbles landing in a Texan's hands could have altered the outcome. All four fumbles going the other way almost certainly would have given the Texans the win.

Another crucial fumble recovery came when Bills running back James Cook put the ball on the ground with three minutes left in the fourth quarter and the Bills trailing 31-30. If the Texans had recovered that, they might have been able to run out the clock and win the game. Instead, Bills offensive lineman O'Cyrus Torrence recovered the fumble and the Bills scored the game-winning touchdown later in that drive.

Bills head coach Joe Brady noted that the hustle of Torrence, whom the team calls Cyborg or Cybo, was crucial to the win.

"We put the ball on the ground there," Brady said. "If our offensive line isn't doing the little things we ask and run to the football, and Cybo doesn't recover that football, and we end up losing that game, a lot of people will point to the fact that we fumbled. And we did fumble. It can't be just because we won the football game that, 'Oh, that didn't happen, we had no turnovers.'"

Brady said Cook was mad at himself for fumbling and that the Bills aren't overlooking how fortunate they were on fumble recoveries.

"He was pissed. I talked to him on the plane. He knows how important he is to our football team," Brady said of Cook. "He understands that when he has the ball he has all of our jobs on the line. He was not happy after that. Even through the win, we've got to clean that up."

Brady knows the Bills can't count on recovering 100 percent of fumbles every week.

item.title: PFT's Week 2 2026 NFL power rankings
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The champs hang on, barely.
item.content:encoded:
1. Seahawks (last week No. 1; 1-0): They can win with Drew Lock. It's unknown how long they'll have to try to do that.

2. Bills (No. 5; 1-0): If winning a regular-season game got Joe Brady to take off his shirt, he'll be butt naked if they win in the playoffs.

3. Bears (No. 6; 1-0): The 59 offense is possibly better than the 46 defense.

4. Texans (No. 3; 0-1): Scoring 31 points should be more than enough for that defense.

5. Jaguars (No. 9; 1-0): They won 34-10, and it felt way more lopsided than that.

6. Ravens (No. 10; 1-0): Derrick Henry may never lose a step.

7. Bengals (No. 11; 1-0): In past years, they would have fully blown a 27-10 lead.

8. Chiefs (No. 13; 1-0): Kenneth Walker III earned every penny of his contract in his debut, and then some.

9. Eagles (No. 8; 1-0): A Week 1 escape vs. the Commanders answered no questions about whether they'll be true contenders.

10. 49ers (No. 15; 1-0): They turned the page decisively on all of those bizarre offseason storylines.

11. Rams (No. 2; 0-1): They're already all alone in last place of the NFC West.

12. Broncos (No. 4; 0-1): Maybe they should have tried to get Drew Brees to come back for last night's game, too.

13. Patriots (No. 7; 0-1): Fortunately, blowing it twice in the same game counts as only one loss.

14. Lions (No. 14; 1-0): The Lions had better hope the Saints are destined to be really good this year.

15. Vikings (No. 19; 1-0): For the second straight year, the Vikings woke up just in time to get a key division win in Week 1.

16. Giants (No. 20; 1-0): Jaxson Dart is the real deal, as long as he can stay healthy.

17. Steelers (No. 18; 1-0): For the second time in three years, T.J. Watt personally delivered a win over the Falcons in Week 1.

18. Cardinals (No. 32; 1-0): Jacoby Brissett is better than you realize.

19. Chargers (No. 12; 0-1): Who's got it better than us? Don't ask.

20. Packers (No. 16; 0-1): Matt LaFleur should be very happy he got that extension.

21. Saints (No. 24; 0-1): They may already be the best team in the division.

22. Cowboys (No. 17; 0-1): Like every year, the offseason's delusion gets a hard dose of reality.

23. Panthers (No. 21; 0-1): The Panthers have only themselves to blame for giving the Bears the pick that became Caleb Williams.

24. Buccaneers (No. 22; 0-1): The Browns are the perfect antidote to a Week 1 clunker.

25. Colts (No. 23; 0-1): They get plenty of hype every year, and they ultimately don't deliver.

26. Jets (No. 29; 1-0): Welcome back, Geno.

27. Raiders (No. 30; 1-0): They started 1-0 last year, too.

28. Commanders (No. 27; 0-1): At least they didn't get blown out.

29. Falcons (No. 25; 0-1): Maybe they should have just kept Kirk Cousins.

30. Titans (No. 26; 0-1): It could be another long year in Nashville.

31. Dolphins (No. 28; 0-1): They aren't tanking; they're just not good.

32. Browns (No. 31; 0-1): Prediction — Dillon Gabriel will be the starter by Week 10.

item.title: Dan Campbell: It's special to be part of first game at new Bills stadium
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Bills will be playing their first regular season game at the new Highmark Stadium on Thursday night and the Lions drew the spot as the guests of honor for opening night.
item.content:encoded:
The Bills will be playing their first regular season game at the new Highmark Stadium on Thursday night and the Lions drew the spot as the guests of honor for opening night.

Lions head coach Dan Campbell said on Tuesday that his message to the team's players about getting the opportunity to be part of the festivities is to "drink it in [and] enjoy this." He also said players will need to take care to avoid being overwhelmed by the situation.

"This will be one of those places it'll be loud. Their fanbase is outstanding," Campbell said, via the team's website. "They are a lot like our fanbase, man. They love it and they show up and they're loud and they're all in and now you're in a new stadium. It's a new environment and this is the first one in that place — the christening. It'll be special. I'm telling our guys to embrace it. Keep your composure. Don't forget it's one play at a time. Stay focused on your job and keep your head about you, but man, enjoy it."

Buffalo would be a tough place to play on a short week in any circumstances, but the atmosphere will be even more heightened for this Lions visit.

item.title: Matt LaFleur saw "protection busts that should not and cannot happen" on Vikings film
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Packers quarterback Jordan Love was pressured relentlessly by the Vikings' defense in Sunday's 39-22 loss, and Matt LaFleur said after watching the film that the pass protection needed to be a lot better.
item.content:encoded:
Packers quarterback Jordan Love was pressured relentlessly by the Vikings' defense in Sunday's 39-22 loss, and Matt LaFleur said after watching the film that the pass protection needed to be a lot better.

"I saw some of the things we have to clean up," LaFleur said. "What’s disappointing is, we had a few protection busts that should not and cannot happen. We knew that was the challenge going in. They were gonna give some tough looks. That’s the toughest test you’re going to face Week 1, to play that defense in that environment. I thought there was some really good stuff, but when your quarterback gets hit 15 times, that's too many times. There are some things we could do schematically that we've got to do a better job with and there are some things we have to go out and execute. But we have to have everybody on the same page if we want to give ourselves a chance."

LaFleur also noted that the Packers' passing game had several explosive plays when they took advantage of the Vikings' blitzing. Love finished with 387 passing yards and an impressive average of 18.4 yards per completion, but ultimately the Vikings' defense got to Love too often.

"We had some great moments when we feasted on it, certainly, but at the end of the game when we needed to make plays, they did what they do," LaFleur said.

What the Vikings do under defensive coordinator Brian Flores is relentlessly pressure the quarterback, and that happened a lot on Sunday.

item.title: Charvarius Ward embraces Guardian Cap in hopes of avoiding another concussion
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: After the 2025 season, Colts cornerback Charvarius Ward said that, if he gets another concussion, he'll "probably retire."
item.content:encoded:
After the 2025 season, Colts cornerback Charvarius Ward said that, if he gets another concussion, he'll "probably retire." To avoid that, he decided to try a Guardian Cap during the Week 1 game against the Ravens.

"I was scared to get knocked out again for real," Ward said earlier this week, via James Boyd of The Athletic. "So I just put a Guardian Cap on. I warmed up with it, and it felt good . . . I just kept it on all game. So I might as well keep it for the season. It's not gonna hurt me."

The real question is whether it helps.

"I don’t know if it made a difference or not," Ward said. "I got a headache right now. I don't think it's a concussion, but it is what it is. It's football, man. You're gonna get dinged up . . . I know what I signed up for."

The full benefits of the Guardian Cap aren't known. It helps with low-impact hits to the helmet. For bigger blows, will it make a difference?

One thing no helmet can do is prevent the brain from bouncing against the skull when the head quickly decelerates. Which is one way to get a concussion.

The NFL has a somewhat complicated relationship with the Guardian Cap. When the device was first adopted for use in practice, the league prevented players from wearing them during games. That position has changed; there are now one or two players in most games who can be seen wearing one.

The league is keenly aware of the aesthetics of the Guardian Cap. They're bulky. They diminish the appearance of the helmet. Even the new model, which doesn't require a cover for placement of logos and stripes, doesn't look the same as the helmet.

As helmets improve, the argument is that they are as effective as prior technology plus a Guardian Cap. But, still, the Guardian Cap will always provide an additional layer of cushioning.

And it's impossible to tell a player who wants to wear one that he can't do it. Even if it doesn't help that much. Even if it can create a false sense of security. Even if it doesn't look great on TV. At this point, if it helps a player like Ward break the tie between continuing his career and not playing, it needs to be among the available pieces of protective equipment for a game that is inherently hazardous to the human brain.

item.title: Eagles restructure Nolan Smith's contract
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Eagles have created some cap space for this season and next season.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles have created some cap space for this season and next season.

The team has restructured the contract of linebacker Nolan Smith. Spotrac reports that converting $1.24 million of his 2026 salary created $992,000 in cap space for the rest of this season.

Smith also had $12.5 million of his salary for 2027 — the Eagles exercised their fifth-year option on his rookie deal — converted to a bonus. That move opened up $10 million in cap space for next season.

The Eagles may or may not have their eye on making an immediate addition to the roster, but the restructuring gives the that option and the extra cap space in 2027 can help General Manager Howie Roseman structure things in a way that keeps the Eagles in compliance with the cap now and in the future.

item.title: Broncos seem to be nervous about a potential Drew Brees tampering case
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: On Monday, Adam Schefter of ESPN reported that the Broncos talked to quarterback Drew Brees about joining the team for the AFC Championship, without acknowledging that Brees's status on the Saints' reserve-retired list made the move impossible.
item.content:encoded:
On Monday, Adam Schefter of ESPN reported that the Broncos talked to quarterback Drew Brees about joining the team for the AFC Championship, without acknowledging that Brees's status on the Saints' reserve-retired list made the move impossible.

What is possible, based on Schefter's report, is a tampering case against the Broncos.

Schefter reported that former Broncos offensive coordinator Joe Lombardi and former Broncos offensive assistant Pete Carmichael spoke to Brees about a potential unretirement. Brees has since told Ed Werder that the former Saints assistants contacted Brees about the possibility. On Tuesday, Broncos coach Sean Payton offered a different version regarding who called whom.

"Drew had reached out, I think, right after the championship or right after the playoff win against Buffalo," Payton told reporters. "I think he called Pete, probably texted Pete or Joe, those guys. None of it even came to my attention. So, when the story came up in Canton, I kept thinking they were just talking about the COVID season. Even in the COVID season when he and I discussed possibly coming back for a Monday night game, he had trouble throwing it. So, I don’t think really anything really came of it. I think in Drew’s mind, there’s that competitor in him. So, I was kind of out of the loop. I don’t think it’s a big story, but nonetheless, certainly one that once they described it to me, it just never got to my level, I guess. He had reached out to Pete, I think, and then Joe.”

Payton is smart. Very smart. The last thing he needs is the league office thinking the Broncos reached out to a player who is technically under contract with the Saints, without permission from the Saints. Even if the Saints don't file a tampering complaint, the league can act without one. For example, the NFL whacked the Dolphins in 2022 for tampering after it stumbled over evidence that Miami had tampered with Payton and Tom Brady while investigating an unrelated matter.

And while it technically doesn't matter if Lombardi and/or Carmichael contacted Brees or Brees contacted them, the situation has a different vibe if someone from the Broncos made the first move without first realizing that Brees wasn't and isn't a free agent.

Time will tell if the league does anything about it. The Broncos' effort to recast the interaction as being initiated by Brees suggests that, at some level, the Broncos are concerned about coming under the inconsistent and unpredictable scrutiny of Big Shield.

item.title: Joe Brady: No concerns about Highmark Stadium field for Thursday night
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The condition of the playing field at the new Highmark Stadium became a talking point after the Bills played their first preseason game at the building this summer.
item.content:encoded:
The condition of the playing field at the new Highmark Stadium became a talking point after the Bills played their first preseason game at the building this summer.

Some players aired concerns about the size and frequency of divots that came up during the course of play, which led the Bills to replace the field ahead of Thursday night's inaugural regular season game against the Lions. The Bills worked out at the stadium on Tuesday and head coach Joe Brady said that the team will not go into the game with reservations about the condition of the field.

“I really don't have many concerns with it,” Brady said, via Jay Skurski of the Buffalo News. “There wasn't a lot of concerns with it the first go around with it in terms of there was stuff that was moving. I credit our leadership that I understand that they want to have the best surface out there and be able to make the decision and kind of go with it. But, yeah there’ll be no concerns come Thursday. Our guys are excited just to be on grass.”

Linebacker Greg Rousseau agreed with Brady's closing statement and said he believes "it'll be smooth" based on Tuesday's experience. The Bills will be hoping that's the case so they can avoid the playing surface overshadowing anything about the game itself in the aftermath of the home opener.

item.title: Ben Johnson suggests he wanted Bears to score 60 points at Carolina
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The Bears scored 59 points on Sunday at Carolina.
item.content:encoded:
The Bears scored 59 points on Sunday at Carolina. Just one point short of a whopping 60 points.

In a Monday interview of coach Ben Johnson on ESPN 1000, Jeff Joniak said this about the 59-37 win over the Panthers: "At that point I was hoping for 60. I was thinking a two-point try at some point."

Johnson paused, smiled, and said, "I don’t think you were the only one."

It's on brand for Johnson. He wants to score a lot of points. He wants to blow teams out. Whenever, wherever, however.

Having a shot at getting to 60 is rare. For the 2026 Bears, it may not be. And there's a good chance that, the next time his team is in striking distance of the number, maybe they will try to get there.

item.title: Jacoby Brissett leads the NFL in passing yards since becoming the Cardinals' starter
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Brissett's 277 passing yards on Sunday helped the Cardinals beat the Chargers.
item.content:encoded:
In Week 6 of last season, Jacoby Brissett started for the Cardinals for the first time in place of an injured Kyler Murray. What Brissett has done since then is something no one would have expected: Brissett has led the NFL in passing yards.

After his 277-yard game in Sunday's win over the Chargers, Brissett now has 3,643 passing yards in 13 games since becoming the Cardinals' starter. That's the most of any quarterback in the league during that time.

Brissett ranks ahead of Jared Goff (3,583 yards), Dak Prescott (3,371 yards) and Matthew Stafford (3,359 yards), who are the quarterbacks with the next-most passing yards since Week 6 of last season.

Although the Cardinals were not a good football team down the stretch last year, Brissett has played well, completing 65.6 percent of his passes, with 24 touchdowns and eight interceptions.

Brissett won't have an easy task on Sunday, with the Seahawks coming to Arizona, but after the Cardinals' upset of the Chargers on Sunday, this Cardinals team may be better than people think, with a quarterback who's better than people think.

item.title: Arch Manning apologizes for "insensitive comment" about AI video from Saturday's game
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Saturday was a good day for Texas quarterback Arch Manning.
item.content:encoded:
Saturday was a good day for Texas quarterback Arch Manning. Monday was not. On Tuesday, he moved to rectify an unforced error.

Via ESPN, Manning apologized for making an "insensitive comment" about an AI video that showed Texas coach Steve Sarkisian violently slapping ESPN sideline reporter Holly Rowe.

At a Monday press conference, Manning was asked if he'd seen any fan clips from the comeback win over Ohio State.

"I've seen a few AI edits of stuff, but that's about it," Manning said. "I saw an AI edit of Sark's interview. Have y'all seen that one? That's a good one. Of him slapping Holly Rowe? It's hilarious."

The remark sparked a backlash, given the jarring video of Sarkisian hitting Rowe.

Manning posted his apology on social media.

"In my press conference yesterday, I made an insensitive comment about an AI video," Manning said. "There is nothing funny about it. It's easy to say I didn't mean it, but I know my words and actions were hurtful to a lot of people. I do not take that lightly and am deeply sorry for that.

"I specifically want to apologize to Holly Rowe for what she has personally had to deal with because of my comments. I have a ton of respect for her and appreciate her showing me grace in this moment. I need to do better and will be more thoughtful going forward."

Rowe accepted Manning's apology.

The unedited video was bizarre in its own right. Sarkisian waited to be interviewed by Rowe and stormed away before she could ask a question.

item.title: Victim in Josh Jacobs case files motion to permanently seal video
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Latest move could make it harder for NFL to see the video.
item.content:encoded:
Previously, lawyers representing Packers running back Josh Jacobs filed a motion seeking to keep evidence in his criminal case from being released to the public. The victim in the case has now done the same thing.

But while the current order is temporary in nature, the new motion filed on behalf of Jacobs's former girlfriend seeks to have the evidence in the case — including a key video — permanently sealed.

Via Rob Demovsky of ESPN, her lawyers said Tuesday that the motion "is consistent with our client's desire to protect her privacy."

The motion complicates the NFL's effort to obtain the video. On Sunday, Ian Rapoport of NFL Network said that the league is "trying all sorts of legal maneuvers" to get the video.

One fairly direct maneuver would be to file an opposition to the motion, with a request for a limited opportunity to inspect the video subject to the requirements of a strict and comprehensive confidentiality order. And the league should ask Jacobs to join in the effort.

Common sense suggests that the harder Jacobs tries to keep the league from seeing the video, the worse to his ongoing career it may be. If the league decides to take an aggressive approach to the situation, the league could tell Jacobs that he'll remain on paid leave until the league processes his disciplinary case — and that the case won't be processed until the NFL sees the video.

item.title: Senate advances the Protect College Sports Act
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: ESPN has gotten its apparent wish.
item.content:encoded:
ESPN has gotten its apparent wish. Partially, for now.

The Senate has passed the Protect College Sports Act, by a vote of 74-24. It's a procedural move and not yet a full vote of the Senate.

The vote comes three days after ESPN put Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas), one of the bill's sponsors, on its flagship college football show to advocate for the passage of the act, without a contemporaneous opposing point of view. And while Stephen A. Smith has apparently chastised me for suggesting that everyone at ESPN supports the Protect College Sports Act, I don't believe that.

It was not my intent to put everyone at ESPN in the same bucket, and I apologize if I created that impression. My point was and is that ESPN's corporate position seems to be that it supports the bill, as evidenced by the fact that two of its most prominent college football analysts (Nick Saban and Pat McAfee) have argued for its passage on GameDay without any real pushback by other panelists, by Disney's reported lobbying for the bill, and by the misguided decision to platform Cruz without offering a voice representing the other side.

Here's a thought — they could have let Smith interview Cruz.

Senator Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) also opposes the Protect College Sports Act. I'll be interviewing him on Thursday morning, for a special edition of #PFTPM.

I'd love to chop it up with Stephen A., too. We agree on plenty of things. On the things we disagree, there's a chance that, through open and honest discourse, we'd better understand each other's points of view. The country currently needs a lot more of that.

The country does not need a federal law that "saves" college sports, in my opinion. College sports are doing just fine, and the system should be required to clean up its own mess without a federal bailout that artificially limits the compensation and freedom of the people who generate the vast majority of the revenue, while leaving unrestricted the ability of coaches to hopscotch the map in chase of their next bag of cash.

item.content:encoded:
There is some positive news on the injury front for one of Kansas City’s top rookies.

Per Ian Rapoport of NFL Network, the current belief is that cornerback Mansoor Delane suffered only a short-term shoulder injury during Monday night’s win over the Broncos.

Rapoport noted that Delane’s X-Rays and CT scans came back clean. Delane was also set to undergo an MRI on Monday.

Delane likely aggravated a previous shoulder injury that he had dealt with during the offseason program and training camp.

The No. 6 overall pick of this year’s draft, Delane registered his first career interception on only his third career snap during Monday’s victory — ending Denver’s first possession.

But Delane landed on his shoulder on that same play, which sidelined him for the rest of the game.

The Chiefs will play the Colts on Sunday night in Week 2.
